blogs.title: The 'Know How' Doctrine: Why Minnesota Employees Can't Sue for Average Daily Wage Penalties Under § 181.101
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Eighth Circuit's strict textualist interpretation of the Minnesota Payment of Wages Act (MPWA). It focuses on the court's reliance on *Allan v. R.D. Offutt Co.* and the maxim that 'legislature knows how' to create private rights of action when it chooses to. By contrasting § 181.101 (which grants penalty enforcement solely to the Commissioner) with §§ 181.13 and 181.14 (which explicitly authorize employee penalties for termination/quitting), the post explores how this decision limits private enforcement mechanisms in state wage laws and reinforces a bifurcated system where administrative agencies, rather than individual litigants, hold the keys to statutory penalties.

blogs.title: Standing in Stalemate: The Mootness Trap When Plaintiffs Are Fully Compensated but Seek Government-Facing Penalties
blogs.description: Focusing on the unique procedural posture of *Cohen*, this article examines the tension between Article III standing/mootness doctrines and statutory civil penalties payable to the state. Unlike traditional damages where full restitution typically moots a case, here the plaintiff seeks penalties paid to the Commissioner intended to deter future conduct. The post discusses the Eighth Circuit's decision to vacate and remand specifically on jurisdictional grounds, analyzing whether a plaintiff retains a 'personal stake' in seeking fines that benefit neither them nor their class, but rather serve as a public deterrent against potential recidivism by the employer.

blogs.title: Procedural Pitfalls: Waiver of Claims and Improperly Raised Requests for Injunctive Relief
blogs.description: While often overshadowed by substantive labor law questions, this post highlights two critical procedural missteps by the appellant that led to affirmance without detailed analysis: waiver due to lack of briefing authority and failure to raise claims via amended complaint. The article breaks down why Cohen's MWTA claim was summarily dismissed for failing to cite supporting authority (invoking *Milligan*) and why his attempt to pivot from monetary damages to a specific injunction regarding policy rescission was rejected under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15(a). This serves as a practical guide for practitioners on preserving claims and avoiding waiver in summary judgment contexts.
